title: Why Seawater Is Starting to Dissolve Seashells | Why It Happens #6

hook_candidates.text: Only air touched this water. Why is this shell dissolving?
Nobody poured acid in this ocean. So why is it sour?
Watch this shell. It's getting thinner by the day.
The ocean is thirty percent more acidic. Where did the acid come from?
You breathe out the gas that's eating this snail's shell.

parts.text: This acid meter is already up thirty percent.
and the snail builds its shell just fine.
Put it back, and it dissolves into the sea
which grab the carbonate shells are built from.
Short of carbonate, the acid eats the shell itself.
parts.tts: Short of carbonate, the acid eats... the shell itself.

sources: Surface-ocean pH has fallen by 0.1 units since the start of the industrial era, approximately a 30 percent increase in acidity: NOAA Education, Ocean acidification resource collection, https://www.noaa.gov/education/resource-collections/ocean-coasts/ocean-acidification.
The ocean absorbs about 30% of the CO2 released into the atmosphere; water and CO2 form carbonic acid, which dissociates into hydrogen ions and bicarbonate: NOAA, same page.

Carbonate ions bond with the excess hydrogen, leaving fewer carbonate ions for calcifying organisms to build and maintain shells; 'If the pH gets too low, shells and skeletons can even begin to dissolve': NOAA, same page.

Pteropod shells placed in seawater with pH and carbonate levels projected for 2100 slowly dissolved after 45 days (shown as an on-screen label, not spoken): NOAA, same page, linking NOAA PMEL's pteropod shell experiment.
Projected surface pH around 7.8 by 2100 under business-as-usual emissions; today's average about 8.1 (meter markings, not spoken): NOAA, same page.
Simplifications, labelled on screen: a simplified model of a sea butterfly (pteropod) and of the chemistry; the 'take the CO2 away' step is a thought experiment for contrast.
